newsitem.title: USA: US options group to cheer growth but trouble looms.
newsitem.headline: US options group to cheer growth but trouble looms.

text.p: When U.S. options industry members meet in Miami on Friday for the 15th annual Options Industry Conference, they are expected to congratulate one another on the industry's strong growth and record volume.

But industry players said the success -- turnover in January reached a record 23 million contracts -- has bred a problem that could stifle that growth. The problem is too much volume on too many listed products.
Michael Schwartz, a managing director of Oppenheimer & Co in New York, said the industry needed to look at delisting inactive contracts to compensate for the explosion of new offerings.

"I even want the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) to sanction discussion for mandatory delisting" of options, he said. "The volume of delistings is minuscule by comparison to the (number of) new listings," said Schwartz, who is also chairman of the industry's Committee on Options.

Edward Provost, senior vice president of operations planning at the Chicago Board Options Exchange, the largest of the four U.S. options bourses, said earlier this week the exchange expects to list around 200 new equity options a year for the foreseeable future.
But some industry participants said that as the number of listed options rises, the quality of the listings declines and many have little or no open interest.
According to some industry sources, up to 40 percent of listed options have no open interest.
Exchanges are hesitant to delist option classes, even if they have no open interest, for fear that another exchange may list them.
"Someone's garbage is another's jewel," Schwartz said. "There has to be more mandatory criteria for delisting."

Harrison Roth, a first vice president at Cowen & Co in New York, said he had suggested years ago that exchanges that delist options receive the right of first refusal for a period of time after delisting to prevent other exchanges from snapping them up.
Industry sources said some price quote vendors are already beginning to cut down on the number of option price quotes they offer and are charging customers extra for more.
"Our biggest concern is the impact that volume has on vendors," Schwartz said.
"One of the big topics these days is the ability of vendors to get out our quotes," said Matt Zahner, a market maker at the Pacific Exchange. "A lot of time is going to be spent on that."
